State the experimental setup and hyperparameters used to produce the reported empirical results: the total number of mobile terminals (MTs) is $U=50$, server selects clients with sampling ratio $q=0.1$ per round (so $K= qU$ expected selected clients), privacy failure probability $\delta=10^{-3}$, number of local iterations $\tau=300$, clipping threshold $C=10$, noise multiplier $\sigma=1.4$, local momentum coefficient $0.5$, learning rate $\eta=0.01$ with decay $0.99$, WT generation learning rate $1.2\times10^{-3}$, $P_2^{fip}=0.1$ for fed-iterative pruning, Fashion-MNIST model specifics and $T=100$, Batch size $B=15$ as used in the experiments; the privacy loss for Fed-LTP is computed using the zCDP accounting expression (Theorem 1).

Summarize representative tabulated results on the Fashion-MNIST private data (Table 3 reported in the paper): on the FEMNIST public/private split in the IID setting, Fed-LTP with fed-one-shot pruning achieved test accuracy $73.65\%$ with cumulative communication $35.30\ \text{MB}$ and accumulated privacy $\epsilon=5.35$, while Fed-SPA with $p=1$ reported $74.40\%$ accuracy but with communication $64.36\ \text{MB}$ and $\epsilon=9.71$, and DP-Fed reported $70.41\%$ with $64.36\ \text{MB}$ and $\epsilon=9.71$; fed-iterative Fed-LTP achieved $72.25\%$ accuracy with $31.66\ \text{MB}$ and $\epsilon=5.35$. These numerical comparisons appear in the paper's result table and quantify the trade-offs among accuracy, communication, and privacy.

Report the utility-privacy trade-off curves (Fig. 3): at a fixed privacy loss $\epsilon=4.0$ the Fed-LTP curves on FEMNIST show approximately $21\%$ and $9\%$ absolute test-accuracy improvements over the baselines in IID and non-IID settings respectively (these percentage improvements are the paper-reported examples from the plotted curves), and the Fed-LTP runs display faster convergence behavior than baselines on the plotted utility-privacy axes.

Report communication-accuracy trade-offs (Fig. 4): for the target $70\%$ accuracy on FEMNIST, the two Fed-LTP pruning strategies required around $22\ \text{MB}$ and $13\ \text{MB}$ (downlink+uplink cumulative) in IID experiments and about $25\ \text{MB}$ and $18\ \text{MB}$ in non-IID experiments (these values are read from the communication-vs-accuracy curves), demonstrating that Fed-LTP attains the target accuracy with substantially lower two-way communication than baseline methods.

Report client resource compression results (Table 2): under fed-iterative pruning with final retention $p=0.20$ on FEMNIST the reported per-client local storage/computation compression ratios $R_{loc}$ across selected mobile terminals include the values $0.44,\ 0.27,\ 0.16,\ 0.10,\ 0.06$ (these concrete numbers appear in the model-compression table), confirming that Fed-LTP reduces client resource usage relative to baselines where $R_{loc}=1.00$.
Table 2

Note additional plotted evidence on the impact of pruning (Fig. 5) and aggregated validation/selection behavior: Fig. 5 shows test-accuracy as a function of accumulated privacy loss $\epsilon$ at several retention rates $p$ for both fed-iterative and fed-one-shot pruning in IID and non-IID settings, illustrating how retention rate, pruning scheme, and privacy cost jointly affect utility; these plots support the claims about improved utility-privacy-communication-resource trade-offs.
Fig. 5

Synthesize the empirical conclusion: across benchmark datasets (Fashion-MNIST, MNIST private with FEMNIST and CIFAR-10 public), Fed-LTP combining server-side LTH pruning, client sparse-to-sparse DP training, DP Laplace validation, and zCDP accounting consistently attains better trade-offs than the baselines (DP-Fed and Fed-SPA) in terms of higher test accuracy for the same or lower accumulated privacy $\epsilon$, lower cumulative two-way communication, and substantially reduced client computation/storage footprints; the reported tables and figures provide numeric evidence for these claims.

Start from the server-side LTH global-model generation procedure (conclusion 2) and evaluate its effect experimentally by an ablation that removes the LTH module (i.e., uses an unpruned/unstructured global model) while holding other Fed-LTP components fixed.

Report the ablation experimental observations (Fig. 6): with fed-iterative pruning, including the LTH module improved test accuracy by about $5\%$ in the IID setting and about $1\%$ in the non-IID setting; with fed-one-shot pruning including LTH yielded test-accuracy gains of about $5\%$ in IID and about $4\%$ in non-IID settings on the FEMNIST benchmark. These numerical improvements are read from the plotted comparison curves that contrast Fed-LTP with and without the global-model-generation step.
Fig. 6

Conclude that the server-side LTH step yields a higher-quality sparse model structure for subsequent private federated training because the ablation demonstrates consistent accuracy improvements across pruning strategies and data-distribution settings when LTH is included.

Start from the DP model-validation mechanism (conclusion 5) and evaluate its empirical effect via ablation experiments comparing Fed-LTP runs with and without per-client Laplace-perturbed validation and server-side selection.

Report empirical results (Fig. 7): across both pruning strategies (fed-iterative and fed-one-shot) and in both IID and non-IID settings on the FEMNIST benchmark, Fed-LTP with the Laplace-based DP validation module consistently attains higher final test accuracy than the corresponding variant that omits the validation module; these differences are visible in the plotted accuracy-vs-privacy curves comparing the two scenarios.
Fig. 7

Conclude that including DP-protected model validation (per-client Laplace perturbation plus server aggregation and argmax selection) improves the final selected model's test accuracy relative to omitting validation, as demonstrated by the ablation experiments.

Start from the zCDP-based privacy accounting result (Theorem 1, conclusion 6) and compare empirically against an alternative "without zCDP" accounting method reported by the authors (the paper's comparison setup contrasts the proposed zCDP accounting to a less tight accounting baseline).

Report the empirical comparison (Fig. 9): runs using the zCDP-based privacy accounting module exhibited faster convergence and better final test accuracy under the same accumulated privacy loss $\epsilon$ in both IID and non-IID settings and for both fed-iterative and fed-one-shot pruning strategies; the paper's plotted curves in Fig. 9 show that the variant without zCDP performs worse in convergence speed and best accuracy.
Fig. 9

Conclude that the zCDP-based accounting yields less conservative (tighter) cumulative privacy-cost estimates for the combined training-and-validation pipeline, which empirically translates into better utility-privacy outcomes (faster convergence and higher final accuracy) compared with the naive or "without zCDP" accounting used as the baseline in these experiments.

open_questions.content: The paper explicitly identifies several scientifically meaningful unresolved issues and directions for future work: (1) Investigate the effect and dynamics of the iterative nature of the fed-iterative pruning procedure across clients under non-IID data distributions, i.e., how repeated, heterogeneous pruning interacts with data heterogeneity and whether theoretical or empirical guarantees of convergence/generalization can be provided in strongly non-IID regimes. (2) Develop and validate generalization guarantees for models produced and selected by the Fed-LTP pipeline on non-IID federated datasets; the current work presents empirical observations but leaves rigorous generalization analysis on heterogeneous data as future work. (3) Study the joint impact of client heterogeneity (differences in computation, memory, and communication capabilities) and downstream (server-to-client) communication cost on overall system performance and fairness of model assignment under fed-iterative pruning; the present experiments suggest these factors matter but do not resolve scheduling, fairness, or optimal assignment policies. These limitations are acknowledged by the authors and remain open problems after this work.
